title: hard c / k sound → ch
rule: the English "k" SOUND (spelled k or c)  →  a throaty "ch"
hook: Zürich German's most famous sound. It's about the sound, not the letter: whenever an English word starts with a hard "k" sound — spelled with a k (king, kitchen) or with a c (cold, come, can) — Zürich turns it into a throaty "ch", like the end of Scottish "loch".

examples.hint: Spelled with a c, but say it: "kome". It's that k sound that turns into ch.
Again a c on paper, a k in the mouth — so it shifts.
I can = Ich cha · to come = cho

title: th → d
hook: English kept the ancient "th" sound; its Germanic cousins hardened it to "d". So a whole pile of "th" words are just one swap away from Swiss.

title: verb + -e
hook: The short, punchy English verbs are Germanic — you can "Swiss-ify" them on the spot. Take the plain English verb and add -e. (Standard German adds -en; Zürich drops the n.)

examples.prompt: Now build it — "I want to learn"

title: p → f / pf
hook: An old sound shift: many English "p" sounds turned into "f" (or "pf") on the German-Swiss side. Once you spot it, odd-looking words fall into place.

examples.hint: Two steps: an English sl- is always written (and said) schl- in Swiss, then p → f.

title: t → s / ss
hook: Another old shift: a "t" sitting between vowels in English often turned into "s" or "ss" on the Swiss side. Once you know it, words that looked foreign suddenly line up.

examples.prompt: Now build it — "I want to eat"

title: -ieren (borrowed verbs)
hook: Long, fancy verbs — the Latin-flavoured ones — usually just take an -iere ending in Swiss (Standard German: -ieren). If you already know the English, you basically already know the Swiss.

title: ou / ow → uu
hook: A neat vowel pattern: where English says "ou"/"ow" (house, mouse, out), Zürich stretches it to a long "uu". Say "loch" with an oo and you're there.

title: i…e → ii
hook: Where English has a long "i" spelled i…e (wine, mine, white), Swiss says a long "ii". Standard German turned the same sound into "ei" — Swiss kept it simpler.

title: make it little: -li
rule: any noun  →  noun + -li  (often with an umlaut)
hook: Not a sound shift but pure gold: add -li to almost any noun to make it small, cute, or friendly — the Swiss do this constantly. Often the vowel picks up an umlaut too.

title: d → t
hook: The mirror of th→d: a plain English "d" often hardens to a "t" on the German-Swiss side. A tiny swap that unlocks a lot of everyday words.

examples.prompt: Now build it — "I want to drink"

title: v → b
hook: Where English has a "v" in the middle of a word, its Swiss cousin often keeps the older "b". Say it slowly and swap the v for a b.

examples.prompt: Now build it — "I want to live"

title: -ght → -cht
hook: One of the most reliable shifts of all: that silent English "gh" in night, light, right becomes a pronounced "ch" in Swiss. See -ght, say -cht.

title: -tion stays -tion
hook: A freebie: the hundreds of English "-tion" words are the same in German and Swiss — just pronounced "tsi-oon". You already own this whole family.

title: -ity → -ität
hook: Another whole family for free: swap the English "-ity" ending for "-ität" (say "-i-tate") and you've basically got the Swiss word.

title: -ly → -lich
hook: English "-ly" endings map neatly onto German-Swiss "-lich". Once you hear it, you'll catch it everywhere.

examples.hint: Swap the stem first: day → Taag (d → t), then -ly → -lich.

title: st / sp → sht / shp
rule: at the start of a word, "st"/"sp" are said "sht"/"shp"
hook: Pure pronunciation, but it makes you sound local instantly: whenever a Swiss word starts with st- or sp-, tuck a little "sh" in front.

title: w = a "v" sound
rule: the letter "w"  →  said like an English "v"
hook: German and Swiss "w" is pronounced like an English "v", so "Wasser" is "Vasser". Small fix, but it corrects a whole pile of words at once.
